Hello all,
I am the Power of Attorney for our dad who has dementia...I live a few hours away from him... My younger brother Paul lives with him and cares for him 24x7 at this point...He has respite care and other assistance multiple days per week.
I pay all of the bills online (that I am aware of), but the problem I currently have is that Paul refuses to send me any of his past mail (which would include any outstanding bills), or any of his spending receipts (which he agreed to do when dad returned to his home from out of state in mid 2024 after being diagnosed with advanced dementia)...Paul was consistently mailing me the accumulated mail and receipts for about a year, but I've received nothing since Sept 2025...I recently put in a change of address for the mail so it will now come to me instead.
Paul also refuses to maintain any or sort of budget in regard to spending, which has been an ongoing issue since he has been an adult (he's now in his mid 50's), which is why I send have sent him a check on a monthly basis that is more than enough to cover daily living expenses...I've tried reaching out to him on multiple occasions to try and resolve whatever differences exist, to see if the financial arrangement needs to be amended, but he refuses to reply because he is of the opinion that he is in charge of everything and I answer to him rather than vice versa.
I reached out to a mediator to try and help put our differences aside, but Paul told the mediator that he would not participate unless I first paid all of his outstanding bills (which I assume means that he has non-agreed to expenditures that are above and beyond the monthly 'stipend' that I send to him).
I believe he takes good care of our dad but I can't go on under this arrangement...I don't want to vindictively move our dad into an adult living center and kick him to the curb but I also can't continue to deal with his lack of cooperation or letting him spend money on a whim as it appears he is.
Any thoughts as to how to handle this situation would be greatly appreciated.
Thanks,
Tom

=== COMMENT 1 (2026-03-17T11:26:01.657-0400) ===
I would not worry so much about the mail. If he was consistently sending mail and receipts to you for a year, and you are paying all the bills online, he may not be receiving any mail other than garbage.
What kind of receipts was he sending, and has stopped? For his expenses?
It's hard to get someone to make out a budget if they never really have. He may find that too difficult for him to do. Maybe you can help him, over the phone, when he claims extra expenses, ask him what they are for. He may find it easier to do verbally, rather than creating a budget or expense sheet.

If he was sending receipts to you for a year, you can go through and figure out the monthly costs for certain common items purchased regularly. Most of our expenses are pretty consistent. For instance, I know from past purchases how much I spend a month on diapers, wipes, gloves, nutrition drinks, etc. I go through the same amount every month. 
I wonder why he is hiding "outstanding bills" that he expects you to pay, but without telling you what they are. He could feel like he's being treated like a child, and resents asking for every cent. If you won't pay for "non-agreed expenditures", does he have any other source of income to pay for his own personal needs? If he is taking care of dad 24/7, he has no money other than what you give to him. 
I would feel better if you paid him an income, through a payroll service, which will take out the appropriate taxes. If your brother continues in this job for years, with a "stipend" for pay, he is losing out on contributing to his own social security account and it will hurt him in retirement. Believe me, this is something I never gave much thought to until I turned 62.

If the mediator is doing their job, they should find a way to bring your brother's issues to the table. Isn't that what the mediator is for?

It sounds like you are trying to manage this from a distance. It might be helpful if you can take a week and go see your brother and your dad. Seeing what their day-to-day is like in person may help you to understand their needs and may even get your brother to open up and start meaningful dialogue with you.

=== COMMENT 2 (2026-03-24T09:16:50.443-0400) ===
Thank you for the update. In my experience with acting as POA, No judge will allow a guardianship to occur if the POA is able to support in written documentation that they are acting in the best interest of the person. Please retain an eldercare attorney to act in your (as POA) and your fathers best interest if you haven't done so yet. This is not a DIY situation and you will pay from your fathers funds as an allowable expense. 

If you still trust your brother to take care of your father, I suggest the attorney create a care giver contract that spells out his duties and pay. 

Best of luck.

=== COMMENT 3 (2026-03-13T16:26:09.140-0400) ===
I would tell Paul that any bills that are outstanding when dad dies will be greatly delayed during the Estate Process so he should keep current with all receipts. 
Also tell Paul that any expenses that are not pre approved will not be paid until they are reviewed by the attorney.

You would also be within your "power" as POA to place dad in a MC facility and sell the house that will help pay for his care. Paul can then find another place to live and have to locate another "gravy train" to supplement his income.

=== COMMENT 4 (2026-03-16T19:14:35.670-0400) ===
Wow. Unfortunately, I think you need to consult with a lawyer with this expertise in their home county. Get someone with a good reputation who isn't going to stoke the animosity just to pad the bill. (This is not necessarily a criticism of attorneys -- sometimes one or both siblings escalate out of resentment and grudges and "I'll show you" and the attorney's job is to do what the client wants.) 

As I think I said before, I suggest that you take the bills and receipts that you already have, and set up online accounts to autopay and pay off past balances (that are legitimate) to demonstrate that you are acting in good faith and don't want your brother's refusal to submit bills to cause deprivation to your dad.

I know a family member who was an excellent caregiver but made a total mess of the finances, fighting against turning over any of that to competent relatives because of ego issues.

It's a shame and I wish you well.

=== COMMENT 5 (2026-03-19T15:33:33.103-0400) ===
First of all - thank God your brother is doing this 24x7. I do the same for my mother with no assistance at all from my two brothers. It is a thankless and stressful job and people do not appreciate the toll it takes on the caretaker. I would attempt to have an in-person visit to the home to visit your parent, see how things are run and have a heart to-heart. It may be that assisted living is the r best option for all - it isn’t really kicking anybody to the curb. Your parent would have more assistance, quality caretakers, meals and socialization with people their own age. It may be that your sibling resents having all the physical caretaking responsibility as it is extremely constraining on one’s life and freedom. Put yourself in his shoes and you might see things differently.

=== COMMENT 6 (2026-03-19T17:14:13.503-0400) ===
I think it is very likely that your brother has high functioning autism or is mentally ill, and that you are asking him to do things he is not capable of doing. A man who is 50's, unmarried and broke has more issues than you realize or want to accept. You should plan to go there for several days and see what's what. Since you haven't heard anything for a long time either one or both may be incapacitated.

While you are there, make a better plan for care for them both. The current situation is untenable.

=== COMMENT 7 (2026-03-13T12:13:20.963-0400) ===
Go to an Eldercare lawyer.
Have a care contract drawn up that is very specific as to what Paul’s duties are and how much he gets paid. Paul should be paid a decent wage for caregiving , not just expenses . You may be surprised at how much Paul should actually be paid.

=== COMMENT 8 (2026-03-13T16:30:33.497-0400) ===
Brother is like Peter Pan the boy who never grew up, and dad either actively or passively encouraged this. You’ll not change him now, but that’s not your job. Your role is to act in dad’s best interests, one of which is to preserve his funds for his care. In your shoes, I’d quit playing brother’s mind games, he wants control, but dad wisely gave it to you. Move dad to memory care near you, sell his house to help pay for it, canceling paying for respite care, and other help. Brother needs to stop using a helpless man with dementia as his piggy bank. I’m sorry you’re in this position, but remember, dad chose you for a reason

=== COMMENT 9 (2026-03-14T12:15:44.003-0400) ===
I am actually pretty surprised at the answers below. You said you believe Paul takes good care of your dad. That is no small matter, in fact it is the most important thing.

Caring for your loved one at home us much less expensive than in a facility. You did not mention whether expenses drastically increased or whether you are just annoyed he stopped sending you the statements.

It sounds to me that sibling issues might be clouding your judgment. Your dad shouldn't be a pawn in this. Your dad made his decisions about your brother and he also decided, probably wisely, to make you POA. It sounds like he was fine with the "mooching."

I am not saying your brother is free to spend all of your dad's money however he likes. But your post drips with scorn for him. I think you should find an eldercare lawyer or a therapist or a geriatric case manager who can help you objectively evaluate the situation.

=== COMMENT 10 (2026-03-16T19:55:45.420-0400) ===
This is all about bills and nothing about care. [member]:
1) How old is Dad?
2) How advanced is his dementia?
3) How able is D to cope with his ADLs? (Activities of Daily Living)
4) How does D get on with Brother? Are they happy with the current arrangement?
5) Does D see this as ‘care’ or as ‘living together’?
6) You “don’t want to vindictively move D into an adult living center” so that you could “kick B to the curb”. How would D react to you moving him to an Adult Living Centre (especially if he could see that it was ‘vindictively’ aimed at B). Or to you choosing to ‘kick B to the curb’?
7) What care does D need? What care is D getting from B? How are any gaps being dealt with?
8) Your monthly payment “is more than enough to cover daily living expenses”. What about payment for care?
9) What is the cost and the acceptability of any alternative care option? Or any alternative co-living option?

It is clear that you don’t like B. It is also fairly clear that B objects to being asked to account to you for what he does and what he spends. You don’t say how D feels, which perhaps matters most.

Have you considered seeking counseling for yourself?

You state that you looked all over for help with this and "finally found some" but is not a lawyer.

=== COMMENT 2 (2026-06-16T22:54:43.000-0400) ===
In Florida, an ex-wife's authority as your Power of Attorney (POA) automatically ends. [1, 2]
Under Florida Statutes Section 709.2109, the moment a petition for dissolution of marriage is filed with the clerk of court, the spouse's authority as an agent under a financial POA is legally terminated. Once the divorce is finalized, her rights are permanently revoked.

=== COMMENT 3 (2026-06-16T19:53:36.000-0400) ===
I have been granted POA in Florida by five people at various times. I have also granted my POA to others multiple times. Florida has strict rules about valid POA documents. First of all, the document has to be signed by the principal (the person granting it) in the presence of two competent adult witnesses. It must then be notarized by a notary public, who can sometimes serve as one of the witnesses. All of these people must be together at the time of signing, and they sign sequentially. The rules must be followed exactly. If they aren't, the POA is not valid. {Chapter 709, Florida Statutes}

Perhaps you have been misinformed about what happened.

=== COMMENT 4 (2026-06-16T18:13:37.000-0400) ===
You don't share what exactly your fathers health issues are, but if he is of sound mind, could he have not long ago taken his ex-wife off as his POA and made you his POA instead, thus saving you both all these issues? 
And of course you can always go to court to file for guardianship for your father which will override any POA, but that does cost thousands to do so.
Until your father changes his POA or you file for guardianship, his ex-wife has the final say regarding your fathers care which of course must be done in his best interests and not hers, and she must also be keeping meticulous records of where his money is going and why. 
It sounds like that's not being done, and I'm having a hard time believing that's there's not an attorney out there that can help you, though if you have no money to pay them it most definitely will be harder to find one, unless they're willing to do it pro-bono. 
Perhaps try checking with some of the Law Schools in your area as they often will allow students to assist in pro-bono cases with the help of licensed attorneys or law professors.
I would also call Adult Protective Services in your area as they have to investigate these kinds of allegations and if need be deal with them to the best of their ability.

My mother, age 79, moved to our property 11 years ago. We moved a manufactured home that she paid for next to us. I naively allowed this to happen and now have regrets and have become resentful as I feel trapped. While her care is somewhat minimal as she lives independently I can see the future and am very fearful. I am 54 and retired 3 years ago and my husband still works, we have two in college and one adult child who is fully independent. When my mother moved here she had lost her 2nd husband and just had hip surgery. Soon after moving to our property she had two knee replacements and two hip replacements. She has never gained a stable walk again always unsteady on her feet. She remarried after being here a few years and we were relieved but then he passed away unexpectedly2 years ago. She then stopped driving. I am very resentful of the 4 hours a week that I run her around or when other appointments come up. I can’t seem to change my feelings towards her and have such difficultly. She was recently diagnosed with a stress fracture to her ankle but can still get around. She is very resistant to assisted living that we can’t afford anyway as she makes to much with social security but not enough to pay a home care provider privately. I had convinced her to accept an assessment for home care services who denied her based on her income. The after being denied home care she asked the doctor for a referral for services because she says her insurance will pay for it but I am skeptical. The referral for physical therapy was approved but not sure she can do much with a stress fracture. I forgot to mention I started working part time just to escape my own brain being consumed by her. Physically with regards to mobility she is not good but manages and internally all her blood work is excellent she only taking celebrex for arthritis which seems to be in all joints. So in summary I feel bad as I don’t do a lot as I have set boundaries —she gets one afternoon a week —but I feel trapped and don’t want to even do that afternoon a week. I don’t see any way out and my husband remains supportive. Also she has no additional support it’s just me. She has life alert and we do leave for a few days at a time as we have an rv. However we know we can’t leave for extended periods of time like we would like too. I feel selfish and guilty all the time. Additionally I don’t have the best childhood history, my history of neglect and her narcissism is very challenging. The positive is she hasn’t become negative towards me and she is always thanking me.

=== COMMENT 1 (2026-08-03T07:44:36.000-0400) ===
Can you consult an elder law attorney or geriatric care manager about the options financially? Care agencies usually have a 3 or 4 hour minimum once a week. I imagine her SS would cover that? You are right to worry about the future as she will definitely become more limited as time goes on. 

Some assisted living places have a plan where a person like your mom can stay for a month if the caregiver is traveling or needs a break. Maybe she would love it and see it as vacation with people waiting on her? 

I know she paid for the manufactured home that she lives in on your property. Could it be sold to help pay her expenses if she moved to assisted living?

What is your goal or ideal outcome other than her being magically out of the picture? Could you explain you and your husband want to spend your retirement driving around the country in your RV for a year and then maybe resettle near one of your grown kids? And that she will need to be in a more supportive setting when that happens? That she has gotten what she wanted /needed these 11 years with your help, and soon it will be time for you to have the same for yourselves? 

it’s good she is willing to do PT. I wish my mom would.

Good luck. I feel for you.

I’d suggest that you and DH decide to move to a different location, or to go on a very long holiday. You say “we can’t leave for extended periods of time like we would like too”. How do you know? Who is telling you? Why tell yourselves something you don’t want to hear?

=== COMMENT 9 (2026-08-02T14:11:00.000-0400) ===
Any living arrangement that’s done can be equally undone. There’s zero sense in you living miserably and resentful. Don’t even consider using your funds to solve this. The mobile home can be moved to another location where mom can pay lot rent to stay. Or you can sell the mobile home and she can move to an apartment. She can use senior transportation services for her errands. A stressed out, resentful caregiver is no good for either of you. Change the plan, it’s not working.

=== COMMENT 10 (2026-08-02T13:56:06.000-0400) ===
I would consult with an elder law or estate planning attorney to number one make sure your Mom has all her legal ducks in a row (like assigning a durable PoA and having an Advance Healthcare Directive and Will) and number two, to see if a QIT will help her get her income lower so she'll qualify for Medicaid. A QIT is a Qualified Income Trust. The money she earns that exceeds the Medicaid limit goes into the trust. At the end of her life if she used Medicaid, the money in that trust is part of the Medicaid Recovery, not inheritance. 

My 97-yr old Mom is on Medicare and has BCBS supplemental gap insurance. Her Internist ordered in-home PT and OT. See if your Mom's primary care doc can do this so you don't have to take her to appointments.

=== COMMENT 11 (2026-08-02T13:30:10.000-0400) ===
“Additionally I don’t have the best childhood history, my history of neglect and her narcissism is very challenging ….”

I think the above quote from your post is key. You don’t mention what your childhood neglect looked like, but I can imagine some scenarios (maybe involving boyfriends, stepfathers?) and it would certainly make me not feel super enthusiastic about arranging my life even only if minimally right now around that person. And it’s great that she’s positive now and thanking you, it truly is, but it can’t make up for her having blighted your childhood, to be blunt.

Some ideas: what if you made the 4-hour driving day every other week? What if you started looking at senior housing for her, and charged her rent so her income would be lower so she might qualify for more things as another person mentioned doing? What if you basically treated her like an older woman who was a renter on your property— respectfully and pleasantly of course but with firm boundaries and assistance to help her find help rather than *being* the help, as one of our regulars here often says?

And when you and your husband want to go on a long RV trip by yourselves you just make sure that your mom has all the emergency numbers should she need them and if needed hires someone to check on her occasionally. Again with her money not yours. 
If and when your mom requires long term care in a facility or at home it will be her money that pays for it not yours as you and your husband will need your money for your own future. And there's always Medicaid when her money starts to run low. 
I guess I'm just having a hard time understanding why your brain is being "consumed" by your mom when you only spend one afternoon a week with her. Maybe I'm missing something here, and maybe you're just not cut out to be any kind of a caregiver even for just 4 hours. I don't know, but what I do know is that we're not hearing the whole story here.

=== COMMENT 14 (2026-08-02T09:13:07.000-0400) ===
Since your mom is cognizant and her "only" limitations at this point are mobility it is time your mom start doing more for herself. 
You have given her 1 day a week, personally I think 1 day a week is a great boundary that you have set. But if I am reading your post correctly you are now regretting that 1 day a week. 

By the way you mention "she is resistant to Assisted living that WE can't afford anyway" YOU and or your husband do NOT pay for her living expenses she is to pay for her living expenses.
By the way if she is not paying "rent" for the property and if she is not paying other expenses if she were to pay her expenses would that result in allowing her to qualify for Home Care. (although from what you have said I do not know what Home Care would or could do for her) And if she says her insurance will cover care whay do you doubt it? Let them asses and let the insurance do what it does. 

Maybe it is time to look into Senior Housing for mom. She would be with others. Some senior housing have "perks" that are not truly a part of the rent but often (at least one of the ones I am familiar with near me) has a rep from a food pantry stop by 1 time a week and drop off items. They sometimes have a drop off of day old bakery items from a local sandwich shop. And all the residents tend to look out for one another. 

Is there a particular reason mom stopped driving? Is she safe to drive? If so that would negate the necessity of you having to give up 4 hours of your week to drive her around. 

More PT should help her mobility once the stress fracture heals but even doing PT while it heals is possible.

Now I am going to be brutally honest and you might want to stop reading here...

You are lucky that you are not a full time caregiver for your mom. 
From what you have written she does not seem to be overly demanding. She is independent save for the fact that she no longer drives. (by her choice) There are Ride Share choices. There are delivery options for shopping. If she is cognizant she does not need your assistance for doctor appointment. 
I think you should be thankful at this point for what you have. 
If you truly want to wash your hands of this Legally evict her from your property. She can take her manufactured home with her and find a place or you can purchase if from her. 
Also you stated that you and your husband leave only for a few days but you would like to go on longer trips away. What is stopping you? If mom NEEDS help she can hire a caregiver for a few hours a week while you are gone, that is all you give her when you are there.

=== COMMENT 1 (2026-10-11T08:52:46.110-0400) ===
Excellent advice already given! But before all that, something else that may buy you additional time... here is what I have found after 8 yrs of full-time caring for my own mother, who has advanced dementia now. Her dementia began at about age 92. She will be 107 in December. And as mentioned in another response, think VERY CAREFULLY whether you are up to caring for her yourself...whether you will be in 8 yrs time, as it does NOT get easier! But...back to "before all that"… Hospitals are good at some things and bad at others. Many, and probably all, suffer from inadequate and overworked staff to properly care for patient load. This leads to (usually unintentional) neglect of their patients, incomplete patient summaries in medical records and missed diagnoses. You might even be surprised and find her medical history might not even mention dementia, which is important for other staff to know! I have found that hospital staff, including doctors, often do not act as if they understand much about dementia. Family members must truly be advocates for their hospitalized loved ones, which means being a "nag" even when you sympathize with the plight of overworked staff! If you think something is "off", be kind but demand answers until you get one that makes sense. The squeaking wheel truly is the one that gets the grease in this case. While dementia manifests differently in different patients, it is typically slow-moving. You describe her as rather suddenly having become "a different person" after being relatively functional even with dementia. If stroke has already been ruled out (and they should be able to determine this), the two red flags would then be Urinary Tract Infection and /or Dehydration. Hospitals can and DO miss checking for these, especially UTI, and both of these cause remarkable mental confusion. Once treated, you may find she is able to return to life before this happened, at least for a time. Demand that she be checked. Then, if she does improve and is able to return home, invest in some indoor cams to place strategically about her house so that you can keep close tabs on her from afar (whether you live with her or not) … thus enabling her to still live somewhat independently. Let her know the cams are there and explain that the purpose is to keep her safe but to enable her to live alone as long as possible. The longer she can maintain independence and stay ambulatory, the more slowly the dementia is likely to advance. Think, "Use it or lose it." Even in their dementia, patients tend to rather adeptly hide their behaviors from others in a fight to remain independent. The cams will give you a view into what's going on when you are not there and you will gain a much clearer idea of her actual needs as dementia advances and a better sense of when it is truly time to place her elsewhere. I have been right where you are; praying for your clarity and strength.

Blondie, 2 different crisis zones (1. Rehab &2. What to do with a house) & you are blurring these as the same problem. They are NOT. The house you can put on the back burner. Focus imo needs to be about getting her into rehab and having her in rehab as long as possible 

If she is currently hospitalized AND she is discharged with orders for rehabilitation, then the discharge planner @ the hospital should be the one that looks for placement for her. Rehab usually done at a SNF aka Skilled Nursing facility with a rehab unit; although there are places that are strictly rehab only and imo you DO NOT want that. The discharge planner may ask you for the name of a place or give you a list of possibilities but really it’s on them to find a spot and submit the paperwork for this as all - !ALL! - her health chart, doctors orders, medication lists, etc are all under the control of the hospital. If she exits hospital having rehabilitation orders this will mean the billing for rehab will be a health insurance benefit. Both her hospitalization and her rehab will be a health insurance policy benefit. 

If she is 65+ then she should have Medicare. Maybe she chose to go from Original Medicare to a Medicare Advantage Plan, but she should have either Medicare are her primary health insurance. Original Medicare will cover the first 20/21 days @ 100% then up to 100 days if their health cart shows this to be what’s needed @ 50%*. The other 50% if on Original is a copay & usually done/paid by supplemental or gap or secondary policy, which covers the copay. If she does not have a gap policy then she’s responsible for the daily copay. 

If she switched from Original Medicare to an Advtange Plan, well they determine what the benefit will be. And the AP tend to be a tight and minimal as possible. Just sayin….

You want her to go into rehab and stay there as long as it is truly feasible. Each day on rehab in some way it’s being paid for by her health insurance. And it gives you another day to figure out just what the next step is best to be…… it also gives you the ability to actually get some rest. I wish I could answer your question, "Am I fooling myself?"
I suppose it depends on what kind of help your mother needs, and for how long, and whether you are up to it.
Medicare is limited in paying for short term rehab (phys therapy) in a nursing home. Once the 20 days are up, she can pay to continue to stay, if you feel that she is benefitting and will benefit from longer physical therapy. This is the time to tap in to her savings, or sell her home, if needed for long term nursing care.

Long term care is a different category than the nursing homes which offer physical therapy, with the goal of preparing the patient to return home to live an independent life (or with family, with manageable care needs).

Yes! You can hire a "nurse for a day" - or something like that. You probably won't have much luck finding someone for one day with short-notice. But, there are home care providers which can offer a variety of services, depending on your mother's needs. It would be best to hire someone to come to the home several days a week, even if for a few hours at a time, just to establish a relationship with a care provider, so when you need to schedule an appointment for yourself, you already have your backup scheduled.

Take a tour of some long term care nursing facilities, or assisted living, depending on how independent you mother is. You may be able to find physical therapists who will come to the home, or she can go to physical therapy as an outpatient.

With her dementia, and sudden weakness, she is not likely to get much better. She will only continue to decline in ability and cognitive function. It is probably time to sell her home to pay for a care facility which can meet her needs. 

IF you feel up to it, you can of course move her in with you, or move in with her, but be prepared - it is Hard work and only gets harder!

This is going to be a lot of work but focus on one single step at a time. You’ll lose your mind if you try to plan the next years before you even have proper diagnoses.

First off you make it clear to the hospital social worker, the discharge planner, the doctor, and anyone else you can find that you are NOT taking her home. Tell them it’s UNSAFE. The hospital social worker, discharge planner, whoever will find appropriate placement. It sounds like they haven’t even figured out her needs fully yet. Often people get discharged to a skilled nursing rehab facility as a bridge between total discharge and the hospital. The person will get lots of PT and OT evaluations there. Once the evaluations are done and your loved one has made as much progress as they are likely to it’s time for discharge. Repeat the step above telling everyone she can’t come to your place because it’s unsafe. 

The rehab facility will find a placement for her and if it’s to a poorly rated and inconvenient location that’s fine. You’ll work on moving her somewhere better and that will be a hundred times easier than moving her out of your house.

Your dad would benefit from a fee-only Certified Financial Planner (CFP) who specializes in retirement income and long-term care planning. Look for someone who charges an hourly or flat fee to evaluate his finances and develop a plan, rather than someone primarily interested in selling investments.

The goal should be to determine how much monthly income he can reliably generate, how long his savings will last at different [member] costs, and what happens when his long-term care insurance benefits run out.

Because his house is in an irrevocable trust, an elder law attorney should also review the trust before any financial decisions are made. The trust provisions and state Medicaid rules could significantly affect his options.

Dementia is about so much more than having a lousy short-term memory. In addition to the executive function issues you are seeing, you would expect to see a loss of empathy for others (understanding you might want to talk to do something together), apathy (where activities that you formerly enjoyed are no longer fun for you) and inertia (loss of the ability to initiate an activity).

Identify resources for her caregiving beyond yourself, .e.g, solicit help from her friends/cousins, check with your area on aging office to see if they offer visitors free of charge, use grocery delivery to cut back on shopping together.

Identify areas of your life that are off limits. My mom was very critical, all her life, about peoples' homes. I could not take her further criticism of mine so we just didn't visit there—ever.

Folks who shop with pwd know that the trip often takes 5X as long—up and down every aisle many times. The small resale shop meant we both could relax a bit and it would be easy to keep an eye on her.

Tell yourself over and over again that none of this is your mom's fault. There may have been trauma in the past; however, this is an entirely new ball game. I agree, all the doctor appointments are unnecessary unless something develops that requires medical treatment. You do not need to agree to the doctor's frequently scheduled routine appointments. They can suggest, you don't need to make the appointment.
I went through this with my husband after he suffered a massive stroke which left him unable to walk, talk, eat solid food, and in diapers. I was seeing a primary care doctor every 3 months, then 6 months, just to follow up, and with every visit I asked "does he need this medication?" or "Why does he need this medication?" and "what will happen if he stops taking it?"
While he was still being treated in the hospital, and subsequently in a nursing home for 9 months, doctors prescribed all sorts of medications, some just to treat the side effects of others. Some were for depression and anxiety. Some for blood pressure, some for high blood sugar, and some just to help with bowel movements, a trouble caused by all the other medications.

I managed to stop them, one at a time, and weaned him off of the addictive depression and anti-anxiety medications ( Celexa and Xanax). That was 10 years ago. He is doing just fine. His blood pressure is good, and stable, his blood sugar levels are in an acceptable range, because he no longer has the stress, is unable to smoke, and his diet is controlled - by me. 
I make him a batch of protein shakes every single day, which he enjoys, and provides all the nutrition he needs. I did meet with a dietician many years ago, which helped me to understand how to meet his nutritional needs. 

I'm sorry you are struggling with your own physical limitations along with lack of good food and help with caregiving.
Is your husband on Medicare? In your financial circumstance, he likely also qualifies for Medicaid assistance. There are dual-complete Medicare Advantage plans which offer perks, such as a healthy benefits card, which helps to buy food and other medical related items needed. My husband has a dual complete medicare advantage plan managed by UHC (in Arizona), and has a healthy benefits card which is pre-loaded with $300 every month that I use to buy Boost nutritional drinks, wipes, disposable pads, pain killers, bandages, and any kind of food. (Except Junk Food) I like salads and lean protein, which I'm able to get.

If he is eligible for any waivered services, Medicaid may also pay for in-home care. Call the county Medicaid office and ask.

I would also suggest finding a medical provider that makes house calls. You can get a nurse practitioner to see him at your home. My husband has had a NP, wound care nurse, x-ray technician, and lab technicians (blood draw) all come to the house. The one thing I would be most concerned with is any complications from his diabetes, if not controlled. So, that might be worth having regular visits from a NP, or at least monitor it yourself at home and call to get a virtual visit or in-home visit if he develops any complications, like wounds on his feet.

Thanks to everyone for sharing your experiences. My husband was diagnosed in December 2024, and one thing I learned very quickly was that you sometimes have to be relentless in navigating the medical system.

I did not rely solely on our PCP’s referral. I asked for a general referral, kept the appointment that was months away, and then started calling neurology offices myself.

At one office, the scheduler told me they had no openings for several months. I asked to be placed on the cancellation list—and while we were still on the phone, a cancellation came in for the very next day!

So my encouragement is: be persistent, stay polite, and keep pushing.

A few things that may help:

Ask your PCP whether they can speak directly with a neurologist if symptoms are progressing quickly or there are safety concerns.

If possible, request referrals to several neurologists rather than waiting on only one office.

Keep the first appointment you can get, even if it is months away, and ask to be placed on every cancellation or wait list.

Call the specialist’s office after the referral is sent to confirm they received it and have everything they need.

Keep copies of medical records, labs, brain imaging, and cognitive testing so missing paperwork does not slow things down.

Be willing to consider another location, telehealth, or an initial appointment with a PA or NP if that can get you into the practice sooner.

Let schedulers know if you can come in on very short notice. Flexibility can make a big difference.

My husband began Kisunla treatment in June 2025 and is expected to finish in December. Kisunla has not been a silver bullet for us, and we have not seen the kind of improvement we prayed and hoped for YET. But we continue to move forward, stay informed, and take things one step at a time.

Most importantly, do not live this journey in fear or shame. Start identifying your support and care team early. Let trusted family and friends know what is happening and allow them to walk alongside you.

Stay positive. Stay connected. Keep asking questions. And keep advocating for yourself or the person you love. ❤️

Therapeutic lies, aka "fiblets", are how most caregivers manage to make the changes they need to make to keep their LO safe. You are being gifted a couple of great options you can build on. Sometimes a PWD will agree to something like a move or giving up driving at some future point and then insist they didn't when the time comes. Sometimes the forget because of short term memory deficits. Sometimes, anosognosia creeps in and they are unable to perceive their impairments and deny needing to move forward with the original plan. In a year, he might not make it easy to move ahead with the plan.

I know you didn't ask, but because you brought it up. 

TKR is not a minor procedure. Two concerns which might not apply here but are worth asking about— what sort of anesthesia will be used and is this an inpatient procedure. There still seems to be quite a bit of variation around this particular procedure. Mom had both her knees done in the hospital as an inpatient with a 2-day stay because of other health concerns. I had my first knee done at a free-standing orthopedic clinic (like a hospital but no ED)— it was "ambulatory" but there was an overnight stay months after mom's second knee with the same surgeon. The second knee was truly same-day with surgery at 1pm and home on my own sofa by 4:30pm. Hospital stays can induce delirium in PWD; even mom (no dementia) had considerable agitation with her second and she's normally the model-patient. If he does stay overnight, you might plan to stay with him.

Most docs use a regional anesthesia with sedation which isn't too huge a burden on the brain. Ask if this can be the case. General anesthesia can cause progression in some people that sometimes results in a lower functioning baseline than prior. Make sure the surgeon and anesthesiologist are aware of the diagnosis. 

The standard for PT is currently 2-3 months post-surgery. Most folks I know are doing 3x weekly the first 4-6 weeks and 2x weekly for another 4-6 weeks. He'll have exercises to do at home during this time and beyond. Assuming he's cooperative, this could be something you segue into a new hobby for both of you. 

Depression is pretty common in PWD. Emotional intelligence (the ability to intuit how others feel about them) and feelings remain well into the end stages of the disease and processing or rationalizing those feelings iisn't really possible anymore which leads to depression as their world becomes smaller. In some people, men especially, depression looks like irritability. Medication can be really helpful with this. 

IME, the rate of progression seems to be different for each PWD. I don't know that depression impacts the rate. That's a good question for his doctors.

There is no point in trying to convince him— in his mind he's the bright and competent guy he always was. To suggest otherwise will not bring harmony to your home.

Taking away driving privileges from our LO’s as dementia progresses is definitely the hardest issue I see discussed on this forum (with the possible exception of end-of-life issues). More than one member has left us in a huff when forum members suggested or even insisted that their LO should no longer be driving. 

My opinion is that driving by PWD should be stopped as soon as dementia becomes evident. Any number of arguments can be raised in support of this.  For example: Your insurance likely will not cover an accident if there is a dementia diagnosis.  The PWD has reduced cognitive abilities, reduced spatial awareness, reduced reaction time.  Getting sued can result in a court case many months later when the PWD has progressed and will appear even more incapable of safely driving. The list goes on.

It can be difficult and cause anger and significant pushback from the PWD. This issue is a major problem particularly for men. It often helps to blame someone else like a doctor for the need to take away driving privileges. A doctor can also help by providing medication to reduce any anger that results.

Caring for our LO’s with dementia absolutely sucks but it is our job to keep them safe and to prevent them from potentially harming others. This is one of the most difficult decision you will have make as a caregiver. I’m sorry that this decision falls on you.

The driving piece is hard. It seems to be especially hard for men for whom driving is intrinsically linked to independence, agency and masculinity. The very last conversation I had with dad, hours before he died, was about me promising to bring him his car (at the MCF) in case he wanted to go somewhere hours before he died.

The driving issue is something of a "unity horse" here and folks— me included— tend to project our own experiences. It's hard, because so often doctors will initially diagnose a PWD with MCI (even when they seem to be more impaired than that) before "upgrading" it to Alzheimer's or some other dementia 6-12 month later. His car was banged up from him having several parking mishaps including 2 garage doors he damaged. It was terrifying. There are specially trained OTs who do driving evaluations which could provide more information in making decisions. Another concern is his insurance. Many policies are voided by driving AMA or if there is a history of dementia or cognitive impairment in his medical record. As you've found logic, explanations, trying to rephrase requests won't get you anywhere. At this stage you can either work around her -hiding & securing things , consider adult day care or care givers in the home to give you a break or consider placement. 

If you haven't already seeing an elder law attorney will give you guidance on the legal papers you'll need and options for getting help with placement costs.

Doing the kind of care a PWD requires in a home setting 24/7 requires mental and physical stamina . Just like some people have the patience to run pre-schools some can handle it ,some caregive their LO after placement - the work doesn't end with placement .  

Both of you need to be safe- keeping you healthy is a part of it too. 

Have you talked to a social worker at the Alz Assoc— they can help  at no charge .
